lines.show: Only 27% of Indian adults are financially literate.
What if every student could live the lesson, before it costs them?
Learning Money by Living It is a pixel life-sim for Grade 11 and 12 students.
A nickname and four questions pick your story: pocket money, a scholarship, or your first job.
Five quick questions set your starting point.
Every month brings a real choice.
Biryani now, or keep ₹100 for tomorrow's cricket?
Pick the impulse, and the Professor shows you why: needs first, then wants.
Then, the phone rings.
Pay up, and the money is gone, and you replay the moment.
The lesson always comes after the choice: money in never needs money out.
Emergencies don't wait for payday.
A small savings jar turns a cracked phone into a bad day, not a crisis.
Without one, the instant-loan apps are waiting.
Then life jumps forward: five years, and a first salary.
That “no-cost” EMI? It comes back every month, right when friends plan a trip.
Start investing at 23, or at 33?
Watch the banyan grow: money that starts early keeps growing on its own.
Every asset is made up, and every number is labelled an assumption. We teach. We never recommend.
In the Charminar Market, students trade shares in made-up companies.
Spread your money, ignore the hot tip, and hold through the crash.
Only behaviour is scored. Never the profit.
Years later, the scams get bolder.
The right move never changes: hang up, and report it to 1930.
At the end, the same five ideas are tested again, asked a new way, so the gain is real.
A one-page report goes to the NGO facilitator.
And their dashboard shows the whole batch at a glance.
